title: Cost Engineering
scopeHtml: Scope: Token economics, routing, caching, batch APIs, budgets and GPU sizing.

notes.title: Token economics
notes.html:
Pricing model. API cost per request = input_tokens × p_in + output_tokens × p_out (+ cached_read_tokens × p_cache_read + cache_write_tokens × p_cache_write). Prices are per million tokens. Facts to know:

  • Output tokens cost more than input tokens, commonly 3 to 5x, because generation is serial and memory-bound.
  • Cached input is billed at a fraction (often ~10% for reads), with a premium for writing the cache (e.g. 1.25x for a short TTL).
  • Reasoning/thinking tokens are usually billed as output tokens even if hidden.
  • Batch APIs often give ~50% discount for asynchronous completion within a window (e.g. 24 h).
  • Images, audio and tool definitions are tokens too.
  • Larger models cost an order of magnitude more per token than small ones.

Per-feature cost formula. cost/request × requests/user/day × users × 30. Include retries, multi-step flows (an agent run may make 10 to 40 calls, each resending context), embedding and reranking costs, vector store, observability, and engineering time.

Worked example. 2,000 input + 500 output tokens at $3 / $15 per million: input $0.006 + output $0.0075 = $0.0135/call. 1 M calls/month = $13,500. Cache 1,500 of the input tokens at 10% price: input becomes 500×$3 + 1,500×$0.30 per million = $0.0015 + $0.00045 = $0.00195 → call cost $0.00945 (30% cheaper). Trimming output to 300 tokens cuts another $0.003.

Conversation cost grows quadratically. If each turn resends the full history, turn t costs ∝ t, so a 20-turn chat costs ~210 turn-units versus 20 for the same turns without history. Hence history management matters.

Real life. A taxi meter: distance (input) and waiting time (output) both tick; rush hour (long outputs) costs more.

Interview angle. Be able to compute costs from token counts and prices and explain which part dominates.

notes.title: Where the money goes
notes.html:
Find the biggest line before optimizing. Instrument each call with feature, user tier, model, prompt version, input/output/cached tokens, latency, cost, outcome. Then aggregate.

Typical culprits.

  1. Resent static context: long system prompts, policy docs, few-shot sets on every call.
  2. Growing chat history resent each turn.
  3. Agent loops: many turns, each carrying all prior tool results; tool outputs dumped in full.
  4. Over-powered model used for easy tasks (classification with a frontier model).
  5. Verbose outputs: chatty formats, unneeded explanations, large JSON.
  6. Retries and duplicates: client retries on timeouts, double-submits, missing idempotency.
  7. Retrieval stuffing: too many or too long chunks.
  8. Unbounded user input: pasted books, attachments.
  9. Abuse and prompt injection driving expensive calls.
  10. Idle self-hosted GPUs.

Methodology. Pareto: usually one feature or one step is 60 to 80 percent of spend. Sort by cost, sample the top spenders' requests, find what is avoidable, estimate savings and quality risk, fix the biggest first, and re-measure.

Real life. An itemized phone bill: you only cut the cost once you see which line uses the data.

notes.title: Cost levers
notes.html:
1. Prompt and context.

  • Trim instructions; replace long examples with a couple of good ones.
  • Retrieve instead of stuffing; cap retrieved tokens.
  • Summarize or window history; drop stale tool outputs; store big artifacts outside the prompt.
  • Put static content first and cache it.

2. Output control.

  • Ask for concise, structured outputs; use max_tokens; avoid asking for explanations when not needed.
  • Use structured outputs to avoid retries from malformed responses.
  • Stop sequences for tool-style outputs.

3. Model strategy.

  • Smallest model that passes the eval; route by difficulty (rules, classifier or a small LLM); cascade: try small, escalate if low confidence or failed validation.
  • Reasoning models only where multi-step reasoning is needed; cap thinking budgets.

4. Scheduling.

  • Batch APIs for non-urgent workloads (nightly enrichment, evals, backfills); combine with caching for repeated context.
  • Off-peak processing for self-hosted fleets.

5. Reuse.

  • Response and semantic caches for safe, repetitive traffic; embedding caches; deduplicate identical requests in flight.

6. Ownership.

  • Distil or fine-tune a small model for high-volume narrow tasks.
  • Self-host open-weight models at steady high volume.

7. Product.

  • Limits by plan, quotas, "regenerate" throttles, usage-based pricing for heavy users.

Evaluate each lever on quality, latency and cost. A cheaper model that causes more retries or human escalation can cost more overall.

Real life. Household budgeting: cancel unused subscriptions, buy in bulk, cook at home.

notes.title: Build vs buy: self-hosting economics
notes.html:
Unit economics. Cost per million output tokens ≈ GPU_cost_per_hour / (tokens_per_second × 3600 × utilization) × 10⁶. Example: GPU $2.50/h, 2,500 tokens/s sustained at full load = 9 M tokens/h → $0.28 per million at 100% utilization, $0.56 at 50%, $5.6 at 5%. Compare with API prices for equivalent quality (a self-hosted 8B model is not equivalent to a frontier API model).

Hidden costs. Engineers (MLOps, on-call), redundancy (≥2 replicas, multi-AZ), idle capacity for peaks, model upgrades, evaluation, security patching, monitoring, storage and networking, and the opportunity cost of building infrastructure instead of product.

When self-hosting wins.

  • High, steady volume that keeps GPUs highly utilized.
  • Data control/residency requirements.
  • Need for fine-tuned/customized/small models, strict latency control, or offline/edge deployment.
  • Predictable cost requirement.

When APIs win. Low or spiky traffic, need for frontier quality, small team, fast iteration, access to latest models and features, no ops capacity.

Hybrid. Self-host a small distilled model for the bulk and call a frontier API for the hard tail; use APIs during exploration and self-host once volume and requirements stabilize.

Decision exercise. Estimate monthly tokens, required quality tier, utilization you can realistically reach, ops headcount cost, and break-even volume; sensitivity-check utilization, since it dominates.

Real life. Owning a delivery van versus paying couriers per parcel: cheaper only if the van stays busy.

notes.title: Budgets, quotas and guardrails
notes.html:
Controls.

  • Per-request: max_tokens, maximum input size, maximum tool-loop iterations, timeouts.
  • Per-user / per-tenant: daily and monthly token or dollar quotas, rate limits, concurrency limits.
  • Per-feature: budgets with alerts and automatic degradation (route to a cheaper model) when exceeded.
  • Global: spend alerts (anomaly detection), circuit breakers, a kill switch per feature.
  • Abuse protection: authentication, CAPTCHAs for public endpoints, per-IP limits, detection of prompt-stuffing and scraping.
  • Runaway agents: step limits, repeated-action detection, cost ceilings per run.

Unit economics. Track cost per active user, per resolved ticket, per document processed, and gross margin by plan. Tie pricing and limits to these numbers. Review weekly; every new feature gets a cost estimate before launch.

Forecasting. Projected tokens = users × actions/user × tokens/action with growth and seasonality; add safety margin; revisit after launch with real data. Negotiate committed-use discounts only after usage stabilizes.

Real life. A prepaid meter that cuts off rather than running up a surprise bill.

notes.title: GPU sizing in one paragraph
notes.html:
Process. (1) Memory: weights (params × bytes) + KV cache (per-token bytes × concurrent tokens) + 10 to 20% overhead decides the minimum GPUs per replica (and whether quantization is needed). (2) Throughput: benchmark tokens/s per replica at your latency SLO with your real prompt/output lengths. (3) Replicas: peak tokens/s required ÷ per-replica tokens/s, add 30% headroom and N+1 redundancy. (4) Cost: replicas × GPUs × $/hour × hours, compared against the API alternative at the same quality. (5) Validate by load testing with production-like traces; re-do after any model, quantization or traffic-pattern change.

Example. 70B model, 4-bit (≈40 GB) fits one 80 GB GPU with ~35 GB of cache (≈100k tokens at 0.3 MB/token); for 40 concurrent 2.5k-token requests (100k tokens) that is just enough; if each GPU delivers ~1,500 tokens/s and peak demand is 9,000 tokens/s you need 6 + 2 spare = 8 GPUs.

Real life. Booking coaches for a trip: seats (memory) and journey time (throughput) both matter.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Economics. Cost = tokens × price, with output tokens 3 to 5x pricier than input, cached reads ~10%, batch ~50% off, and thinking tokens billed as output. Multi-turn and agentic flows multiply context resending (quadratic history cost).

Diagnosis. Instrument per call and per feature; one or two steps usually dominate the bill. Typical culprits: resent static context, long history, agent loops, over-sized models, verbose outputs, retries, retrieval stuffing, abuse.

Levers. Trim prompts, retrieve not stuff, cache prefixes, constrain outputs, right-size and route models, cascade to larger models only on failure, batch offline work, reuse via caches, distil or self-host at volume, and use product limits.

Self-hosting. Cost per token ≈ GPU $/hour ÷ effective tokens/hour; utilization dominates; add ops costs; wins at steady high volume or strict data control; hybrid designs are common.

Controls. Per-request caps, per-user and per-feature quotas, anomaly alerts, kill switches, agent step limits, forecasting, and unit-economics tracking.

Sizing. Memory first (weights + KV + overhead), then benchmarked throughput at the SLO, then replicas with headroom and redundancy.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Cost is tokens times price, and output tokens are the expensive ones."
  • "Measure by feature; the Pareto top item pays for the whole project."
  • "Utilization, not list price, decides build versus buy."
  • "Every cost cut must pass the quality eval, or it is just a bug that saves money."
